10210-wolves-of-the-sea-being-a-tale-of-:
Randall Parrish published this sea novel in 1918, setting it in the days of the early American colonies. Its narrator, Geoffry Carlyle, is a seaman who tells his own story in the first person, looking back on youth, danger, and a woman he never forgot. The tale moves from English jails and forced labor to ships off Virginia and the Chesapeake.

Carlyle is sent into servitude, held on a prison ship, and then drawn aboard the pirate craft Namur, where Dorothy Fairfax is also at risk. Mutiny, murder, escape in an open boat, a slaver, and a hunt for treasure follow, chapter by chapter. Readers get a fast, old-style adventure of loyalty, daring, and love at sea.
23691-archeological-expedition-to-arizon:
Jesse Walter Fewkes wrote this report of his 1895 expedition to Arizona for the Bureau of American Ethnology. It surveys ancient ruins in two regions: the Verde Valley and Tusayan, the Hopi country. Fewkes maps, measures, and classifies what he finds, and sets down the stories told about each place.

Verde Valley sites include Montezuma Well, the cliff houses of the Red-rocks, Palatki, and Honanki, with the objects found there. In Tusayan he treats the Middle Mesa and East Mesa ruins, the legend of Awatobi's destruction, and the great pueblo of Sikyatki. Pottery, stone tools, bone objects, shrines, and prayer-sticks all get careful chapters, making this a foundation record of Southwest archaeology.
24583-langstroth-on-the-hive-and-the-hon:
The Reverend L. L. Langstroth wrote this bee-keeper's manual, published at Northampton by Hopkins, Bridgman. Its title page shows the queen, the worker, and the drone, with bees surrounding their queen as she rests upon the comb. Langstroth, the inventor of the movable-frame hive, wrote for keepers who wanted healthy bees and good honey.

Chapters cover the hive, the honey-bee's life, swarming, feeding, and the care of colonies through the seasons. Langstroth quotes Shakespeare on bees teaching order to a peopled kingdom. His manual remains the founding book of modern beekeeping, practical, clear, and still read by keepers today.
24956-live-to-be-useful-or-the-story-of-:
Thomas Nelson and Sons' 1913 story follows Annie Lee, a girl crippled from her eighth summer who endures five years of pain with devout cheerfulness. Rather than sinking into self-pity, Annie consoles her parents and turns her sickroom into a place of comfort for others. Her faith steadies the household, and her patience becomes a quiet lesson for everyone around her.

Irish nurse Annorah tends Annie with warmth and plain sense, while Biddy Dillon's lame boy Phelim finds in Annie a fellow sufferer who understands him. A priest disputing with Annorah adds a note of doctrinal debate to the household scenes. The book's moral is in its title: usefulness, not health or fortune, gives a life its worth.
25200-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-volum:
The Index to volume 17 of Chambers's Edinburgh Journal covers numbers 418 to 443, from January to June 1852. William and Robert Chambers conducted the journal from London and Edinburgh, and this volume's index maps every article to its page.

Entries range from familiar sketches and moral essays to notes on Liberia, Nantucket sea-kings, South African reptiles, and the thinness of a soap bubble. A transcriber's cross-reference ties each issue number to its dates and pages. The index itself is a useful guide to what a popular Victorian weekly offered its readers.
britannica-1911-ainu:
Ainu, a people of Japan's northernmost islands, are treated at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Their name means man in their own tongue. Little is known for certain about their earliest history. Careful research, the entry argues, shows they were immigrants rather than Japan's first inhabitants, reaching Yezo by way of the Kurile islands.

Crossing the Tsugaru strait, the Ainu once settled much of Japan's main island, displacing a small pit-dwelling people they called koro-pok-guru. The Japanese, arriving from the south and west, later drove the Ainu north into Yezo, the Kuriles, and southern Sakhalin. The entry then covers their beliefs, including a supreme Creator alongside sun, moon, water, and mountain gods. It also pictures their world resting on a great fish whose movements cause earthquakes, a fancy likely borrowed from the Japanese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-laws-of-m:
Ancient India's sacred law book, the Manava Dharma-sastra, is introduced here under its English name, the Laws of Manu. Brahmins revere it highly and credit it with divine origin and remote antiquity. Its reputed author, Manu, survived the Flood as father of humanity and now enjoys in heaven the rank of an all-knowing deity.

Ten great sages approached Manu and asked him to declare the sacred laws of the castes. He answered by having Bhrigu, carefully taught in the metrical institutes, deliver the instruction. So the work claims to be Manu's dictation through Bhrigu, learned in turn from self-existent Brahma. Contents, castes, duties, and penalties follow in outline.
doe-osti-2588116-los-alamos-national-lab:
Leslie Hansen, Sonja Salzman, Ashley Kowalewski, and four colleagues prepared the Los Alamos National Laboratory 2024 Annual Site Environmental Report, LA-UR-25-27701, issued September 11, 2025. Federal orders require this report every year. It is the laboratory's public account of how its operations affected the environment around Los Alamos, New Mexico, during 2024, written under federal plain language rules.

Eight chapters structure the account: a compliance summary, environmental programs and data quality, air quality, groundwater protection, watershed quality, ecosystem health, and public dose and risk. Monitoring covers radioactive air emissions, chemicals and radionuclides in storm water, sediment, soil, plants, and animals. One thread follows the site's chromium plume work. A review team of 15 subject matter experts met in March 2024 to evaluate the interim measures and characterization. The New Mexico Environment Department wrote to the Department of Energy that May.
doe-osti-2589452-princeton-plasma-physic:
Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory report PPPL-2025_633 is the site's Annual Site Environmental Report for calendar year 2024. Authors Mark Hughes, Michelle Turnbach, Joseph Hornsby, and co-authors cover the fusion research laboratory in Princeton, New Jersey, run by Princeton University under contract DE-AC02-09CH11466.

Chapters describe the site setting, its fusion operations, and the monitoring that surrounds them. Radiation levels from operations stayed very low. The site's goal for the highest individual worker exposure was under 100 millirem per year above natural background. Tables track water use, permit reporting, and waste shipments for the year. The volume serves as the laboratory's public environmental record, showing regulators and neighbors what was measured and what left the site in 2024.
doe-osti-3000215-optimizing-geospatial-a:
Scott Parent, Benjamin Blakely, Julie Muzzarelli and co-workers at Argonne National Laboratory examine language models as safeguards helpers, in ANL-25/60. International nuclear inspectors must place reported activities on the map, drawing on multilingual news and commercial satellite data that grow faster than analyst teams. Large language models can surface places, events and links quickly, but their answers wobble: place names repeat across countries, descriptions are vague, and false leads waste scarce inspection effort.

The project tested methods to ground model output so every location claim can be checked. Its conclusions demand explicit, layered validation: consistency checks, corroboration against knowledge bases, and cross-checks with satellite imagery where possible. Scoring must also be spatially aware, catching geographic bias rather than counting simple hits. With constraints doing the guard work against invented detail, such tools could speed state evaluations and access planning while keeping judgements traceable.
doe-osti-3014425-enabling-the-broader-us:
Coreform Inc.'s final report for SBIR award DE-SC0020906 was submitted January 26, 2026. Robert Carlsen was principal investigator, and Michael Scott the submitting official. The project covers enabling broader use of MOOSE. MOOSE is Idaho National Laboratory's multiphysics simulation framework. It is powerful, but building good finite element meshes for complex parts is hard work. That work gates who can use it. Coreform's Phase IIA project built geometry tools to lower that gate.

The workflow processes large, detailed assemblies. It skips the traditional labor-intensive meshing pipeline. A worked example simulates flex cables. It finds the bending radius that prevents delamination over decades of service. Compile tests and demonstrations on complex geometries fill the accomplishments section. The project period ran August 2023 to August 2025. It targets nuclear energy users and other simulation communities.
doe-osti-3015962-efficient-silicon-carbi:
General Atomics' final technical report for award DE-EE0010209, submitted January 15, 2026. It covers work led by principal investigator Ivan A Ivanov, with Nicole Pacheco as program manager. Hesham E Khalifa is also named on the record. Partners were the Nonwovens Institute at North Carolina State University and Harper International. The goal was a cheaper, continuous way to make silicon carbide fiber, a strong ceramic fiber for very hot parts.

The team processed new precursor materials, the polymer strands that become ceramic fiber, using changed material handling, and ran both coil and spool routes. Reported fiber properties met or beat the program targets in the report's own tables for both routes. Sections walk through curing of the polycarbosilane polymer, results by budget period, and key achievements. Manufacturers get a tested route toward making this fiber in long, continuous runs instead of small batches.
doe-osti-3016053-research-traineeship-fo:
Yale University's Wright Laboratory final report on its Research Traineeship for Diversity in Nuclear Physics was led by Karsten M Heeger, with Reina H Maruyama as co-investigator. The grant aimed to train and keep a diverse group of future nuclear physicists. It focused on undergraduates from underrepresented, first-generation, and low-income backgrounds.

The program offered a year-long research experience and a summer research and training program. Workshops, professional skills training, and personal mentoring supported the students. It also plugged them into the national nuclear physics community. Two postbaccalaureate trainees are profiled by name, and one profile follows simulation and measurement work for a tritium spectroscopy experiment. The report shows how a leading research lab can widen the path into physics careers.
doe-osti-3374639-configurations-of-comme:
Report INL/RPT-23-74632 from Idaho National Laboratory, dated July 2025, lays out workable setups for commercial nuclear power at sea. The lead authors are Sanjay Mukhi, Abdalla Abou Jaoude, and Levi Larsen. The report is the second deliverable of a Department of Energy award led by the American Bureau of Shipping. That award aims to speed demo projects for advanced reactors in maritime use.

The team scores reactor types against four classes of use. The classes run from fixed offshore plants to ships that sail worldwide. Light-water reactors already serve in naval ships, so they score well for self-propelled roles. Small modular designs fit fixed coastal sites with grid ties. Salt-based and water-based small reactors also suit ocean-going ships. Sodium-cooled fast reactors rate poorly, in part due to sodium-water reaction risks.
podcast-tuckercarlson-XS7itdfgNnU:
Tucker Carlson questions former governor Mike Huckabee in a tense interview about the United States and Israel. The episode title calls the bond between the two lands toxic. Huckabee is a strong backer of Israel, which sets up a sharp clash with his host.

Carlson presses Huckabee on foreign aid, war, and how faith shapes views of Israel. Huckabee defends the bond and his own role in it. The heat in the room is the point of the episode. Listeners can hear two men on the same broad side of politics split hard over one country and what America owes it.
wolves-of-the-sea-being-a-tale-of-the-co: Randall Parrish wrote this 1918 sea adventure set in colonial times. Pages present here hold the title page and part of a chapter list, but no story text. The title page frames the tale as a seaman's own record. Geoffry Carlyle tells of strange adventures aboard a pirate craft called the Namur. Chapter titles name a prison ship, Dorothy Fairfax, the shores of Virginia, and a swim to the pirate ship. The narrative itself does not appear in these pages.
